title: First words
goal: Greet people, ask how they are, say yes, no, thank you and sorry, and choose the right word for 'you'.
intro:
Welcome to Nepali! In this unit you'll learn the words you'll hear a hundred times a day in Nepal: नमस्ते, हजुर, हो, होइन, धन्यवाद. You'll also meet the most important social idea in Nepali grammar: there are **four words for 'you'**, from intimate तँ to very respectful हजुर, and the verb changes with each one.

Read with the romanization at first, listen, and repeat out loud. Remember that plain *a* is a short, rounded 'uh/o' sound: नमस्ते is 'no-mos-te'.

vocab.en: hello; goodbye (respectful, any time of day)
vocab.note: Said with palms pressed together. Works as hello and goodbye, to anyone.
Speeches, TV, offices, greeting a group.
Reply 'हजुर?' when someone calls you, or to mean 'pardon?'. Also a very respectful 'you' for elders (takes तपाईं verb forms).
Answers questions with हो: 'Is it…?' → हो 'It is.'
Negative of हो.
The standard 'yes' to a request or offer. Literally 'it happens/it will be'.
Informal; with friends and family.
Said to elders or a boss: 'very well'.
Used with strangers and in shops/offices. Between family and close friends thanks are rarely spoken.
Very common among younger urban speakers.
माफ गर्नुहोस् 'excuse me / sorry' (polite).
Common in casual speech.
ठीक छ 'it's fine'; ठीकै 'so-so, alright'.
सन्चै (sanchai) = 'quite well'. सन्चै हुनुहुन्छ? 'Are you well?' is the classic polite greeting.
मज्जामा छु 'I'm doing great'. मज्जा आयो 'that was fun'.
At the start of a sentence it can mark a yes/no question: के तपाईं नेपाली हो?
के छ खबर? 'What's the news?' = 'How's it going?'
Forms: म छु, तिमी छौ, ऊ छ, उनीहरू छन्; polite तपाईं हुनुहुन्छ. Negative छैन. See grammar.
Only for very close friends, small children, animals — or to insult. Avoid as a learner.
Friends, people younger than you, children, partners.
The safe default with adults you don't know, anyone older, officials, shopkeepers.
Comes after the word it refers to: म पनि 'me too'.
राम्रो छ 'it's good/nice'.
फेरि भेटौँला 'see you again' (lit. we'll meet again).

vocab.en: OK then; here you go; right!
vocab.note: Used when handing something over, wrapping up, or urging: ल, जाऊँ 'OK, let's go'.
Mostly on signs and in formal requests. In speech, politeness comes from the verb form (दिनुहोस्) instead.
स्वागत छ! 'Welcome!'
In set phrases: शुभ प्रभात 'good morning', शुभ रात्रि 'good night', शुभ यात्रा 'bon voyage'. Mostly formal or written.

phrases.en: Yes please, thank you. (accepting an offer)

phrases.note: Lit. 'Shall I go, then?' — the normal way to take your leave.

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last
grammar.body:
Nepali sentences are **Subject – Object – Verb**. Whatever else happens, the verb goes at the end: 'I tea drink', 'I fine am'.

There are no words for 'a' or 'the'. To make a yes/no question you simply raise your voice at the end — or, optionally, put के at the start. Short answers repeat the verb: तपाईं सन्चै हुनुहुन्छ? → सन्चै छु 'I'm well'.

The pronoun is often dropped when it's obvious: सन्चै छु 'I'm well' (the ending -छु already tells you it's 'I').

examples.en: I am fine. (lit. I fine am)
I drink tea. (lit. I tea drink)
Are you well? (with question marker के)

grammar.title: Four ways to say 'you' — and the verb changes
grammar.body:
Nepali grades 'you' by respect, and the **verb ending changes to match**. With छ 'is/am/are':

**तँ** *taṃ* (intimate/rude) → **छस्** *chhas*
**तिमी** *timi* (familiar) → **छौ** *chhau*
**तपाईं** *tapāiṃ* (polite) → **हुनुहुन्छ** *hunuhunchha*
**हजुर** *hajur* (very respectful) → **हुनुहुन्छ** *hunuhunchha*
and **म** *ma* 'I' → **छु** *chhu*

Notice that the polite form isn't a version of छ at all: it is built from हुनु 'to be' + the honorific ending -नुहुन्छ. Every verb has this polite form (खानुहुन्छ 'you eat', जानुहुन्छ 'you go'), and you'll use it constantly.

**Which to use?** Use **तपाईं** with every adult you don't know well, anyone older, and in shops and offices. Use **तिमी** with friends your age, younger people and children. Leave तँ alone for now. हजुर is used for parents-in-law, grandparents, teachers, and as a respectful reply word.

examples.en: How are you, mate? (very close friend only)
Are you well? (very respectful, e.g. to a grandparent)

dialogue.title: Good morning, neighbour
dialogue.setting: Sarah, a volunteer living in Kathmandu, meets her neighbour Sita (an older woman, so Sarah calls her दिदी 'big sister') outside the house.

lines.speaker: Sita
lines.native: म पनि ठीक छु। चिया खानुहुन्छ?
lines.roman: ma pani ṭhik chhu. chiyā khānuhunchha?
lines.en: I'm fine too. Will you have some tea?

lines.speaker: Sita
lines.en: Here you are — you're welcome here.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: माफ गर्नुहोस्, अब जाऊँ है त?
lines.roman: māph garnuhos, aba jāuṃ hai ta?
lines.en: Sorry, I'd better be off now, OK?

culture: **नमस्ते** with palms together is the all-purpose greeting; with elders, bow the head a little more. Instead of asking 'how are you', Nepalis very often greet each other with **खाना खानुभयो?** 'Have you eaten (your rice)?' or **कता हिँड्नुभयो?** 'Where are you off to?' — these are friendly openers, not real questions. People are addressed by kinship terms rather than names: an older woman is **दिदी**, an older man **दाइ**, a younger person **भाइ/बहिनी**, even if you're not related. And when someone calls your name, the polite answer is not 'what?' (के?) but **हजुर?**
